paras: The attempted lynching of Bill Grant took place at Bainbridge, Georgia, on the night of July 16, 1903, when a group of men held up a deputy sheriff, demanded the keys to the county jail and gathered with threats near the railroad depot. Grant, a Black prisoner, had been sentenced to hang for the murder of a white man and had just been granted a new trial. The sheriff called out the local military company, which guarded the jail with sworn deputies, and Grant was not harmed.

Grant had been convicted at the last term of court of the murder of Jim Bird, a white farmer killed near Climax during the Christmas holidays of 1902. According to the Savannah Morning News, a motion for a new trial had been granted, and the ruling "created intense feeling in this immediate territory."

About 11 o'clock that night, Deputy Sheriff Dean was returning from a failed attempt to arrest another man, wanted for assault with attempt to murder, when "four unknown persons" stopped him and demanded the jail keys. When Dean said he did not have them, the men ordered him to get them from the sheriff. Dean reported to the sheriff and then found the group near the Atlantic Coast Line depot, where its number had "alarmingly increased" and threats were made.

Some at first believed the crowd wanted a man named Thrash, who had eloped that week with the wife of a railroad shop foreman, but the dispatch reported that "developments proved that Bill Grant was the man wanted." Sheriff Fordham asked Capt. Flemming to order out the Bainbridge military company, and armed militia and citizens sworn as deputies surrounded the jail. Guards were alarmed during the night by "suspicious persons skirting the premises," and heavier guards were planned for the next night.

No report of arrests or of the identity of the men who stopped the deputy appears in the coverage. Grant was hanged in the county jail at Bainbridge on December 18, 1903, for Bird's murder, with only officers and reporters admitted. He "protested his innocence to the very last," and a large crowd of Black residents stood outside the jail until his body was brought out at noon, while "everything passed off very quietly."

The Savannah Morning News carried the fullest account on July 18 under stacked headlines, "TROOPS ON GUARD" and "BAINBRIDGE EXCITED BY DEMANDS OF A MOB," and described the night as "an attempt probably to lynch." Its report named Grant and the officers but gave no description of the men in the mob and offered no comment on them.

Elsewhere the episode survived only as a single unnamed line in a syndicated news summary, run by the Bamberg Herald in South Carolina on July 23. The Black Savannah Tribune printed the same line word for word on July 25, among other briefs and without comment. The white press reported Grant's December execution as "HANGED FOR MURDER" and "Negro Murderer Hanged," without reference to the July mob.

The syndicated brief placed the calling out of troops at an early hour on Saturday morning, July 18, while the Bainbridge dispatch, already in print that Saturday, described the events as having occurred "last night" in a report dated July 17.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Bill Grant
bases: Men demanded the jail keys from a deputy and a growing crowd made threats in what the Savannah Morning News called 'an attempt probably to lynch' a jailed prisoner, Bill Grant; no one was harmed (A1, A2).

Four men, then a larger crowd, sought without authority to take Grant, held for the murder of a white man, from jail, but militia guarded it and no one was killed (A1, A2); Grant was later hanged legally (A5, A6), so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The Savannah Morning News dispatch (A1) and a separately worded syndicated brief (A2, reprinted in A3) agree that a mob held up a deputy, demanded the jail keys, and that troops guarded the jail, though the brief may rest on the same original dispatch.

accounts.label: Bainbridge dispatch
accounts.gist: Four unknown men held up the deputy and demanded the jail keys; a growing crowd made threats near the depot; the mob wanted Grant, whose new trial had 'created intense feeling', and the sheriff called out the militia.

accounts.label: Syndicated news brief
accounts.gist: Troops were called out early Saturday morning to protect the Bainbridge jail from a mob that had held up a deputy and demanded the keys.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News stacked headlines on the guard and the mob's demands ('TROOPS ON GUARD', 'BILL GRANT WAS THE MAN THE MOB SOUGHT') and called the night 'an attempt probably to lynch', without editorial comment.
The Bamberg Herald ran the episode as one line in its 'Cream of News' summary.
The Savannah Tribune ran the same one-line brief in its column of news items, with no names and no comment.

versions.value: Night of July 16 ('last night' in a dispatch dated July 17)

conflicts.note: The Bainbridge-datelined dispatch, already published on July 18, is the better evidence for the night of July 16-17; the syndicated brief may have taken the day from the Savannah paper's Saturday publication date.
